beats: To save this cracked part, you remove even more of it.
You drill a hole right at the crack's tip, and it stops growing.
Every time this panel is pulled, force flows through it like water.
The crack blocks that flow, so the force squeezes around its end.
And a crack's end is incredibly sharp, almost no width at all.
The sharper the corner, the more force piles up in one tiny spot.
At that tip, the plastic carries dozens of times the average stress.
So it tears a little further, every single time it's pulled.
Now drill a three millimetre hole, an eighth of an inch, just past the tip.
The sharp point is gone, replaced by a wide, round edge.
Force now flows smoothly around the hole, at only about three times the average.
Less plastic, but no sharp tip. The crack has nothing left to grow from.
That's why cracks almost always start at sharp corners, never at smooth curves.
Cogwise: how things work. Follow for the next one!
